title: Torque and Rotational Dynamics
short_intro: Torque is the rotational analogue of force, defined as the cross product of the position vector and the applied force about a given point or axis. It measures the effectiveness of a force in producing rotational acceleration about an axis of rotation.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of torque, relation with angular acceleration, principle of moments, conditions for static equilibrium of rigid bodies.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Vector formulation, torque in polar coordinates, central forces, torque on a current loop, torque about a moving point, and Lagrangian formulation.

prerequisites: Centre of mass and moment of inertia

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Significance
bullets: Torque (tau) is a vector quantity that represents the turning effect of a force.
It depends on the magnitude of the force, the moment arm (perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force), and the angle between them.
The SI unit of torque is Newton-metre (N·m) and its dimensional formula is [M L<sup>2</sup> T<sup>-2</sup>].

concept_notes.heading: Torque and Angular Acceleration
bullets: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the net external torque is equal to the product of the moment of inertia (I) and the angular acceleration (alpha).
Expressed as tau = I alpha, this relation is the rotational counterpart of Newton's second law (F = ma).
If the net external torque acting on a system is zero, the angular acceleration is zero, leading to a constant angular velocity.

concept_notes.heading: Conditions for Static Equilibrium
bullets: For a rigid body to be in complete mechanical equilibrium, both the vector sum of all external forces and the vector sum of all external torques about any point must vanish.
Sum of forces: Sigma F = 0 ensures translational equilibrium.
Sum of torques: Sigma tau = 0 ensures rotational equilibrium.

concept_notes.heading: Torque due to Central Forces
bullets: A central force is directed toward or away from a fixed center point, and its line of action passes through that center.
Since the position vector and the central force are collinear (angle is 0 or pi radians), the torque exerted by a central force about the center of force is identically zero.
Zero torque implies the conservation of angular momentum for any particle moving under a central force field.

derivations.title: Relation between Torque and Angular Momentum
derivations.conditions: Particle or system of particles with respect to a fixed origin
steps: Start with the definition of angular momentum L = r x p = r x (mv).
Take the time derivative of angular momentum: dL/dt = d/dt (r x p) = (dr/dt x p) + (r x dp/dt).
Recognize that dr/dt = v and p = mv, so dr/dt x p = v x (mv) = 0 because a vector cross product with itself is zero.
Substitute dp/dt = F (Newton's second law) into the second term: r x (dp/dt) = r x F = tau.
Conclude that the time rate of change of angular momentum equals the net external torque acting on the system: dL/dt = tau.

derivations.title: Work Done and Power in Rotational Motion
derivations.conditions: Rigid body rotating about a fixed axis under constant or variable torque
steps: Express the infinitesimal work done by a torque as dW = tau d(theta), where tau is torque and d(theta) is angular displacement.
Integrate the work from an initial angle theta<sub>1</sub> to a final angle theta<sub>2</sub>: W = integral from theta<sub>1</sub> to theta<sub>2</sub> of (tau d(theta)).
To find rotational power (P), differentiate work with respect to time: P = dW/dt = tau (d(theta)/dt).
Substitute angular velocity omega = d(theta)/dt into the power equation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torque vs. Angular Acceleration Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin with Torque (tau) on the vertical axis and Angular Acceleration (alpha) on the horizontal axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of this linear graph directly yields the Moment of Inertia (I) of the rotating body.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually to find moment of inertia from experimental data or theoretical curves.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searle's or Flywheel Apparatus Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic diagram of a heavy flywheel mounted on horizontal frictionless bearings with a cord wound around its axle carrying a hanging mass.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to determine the moment of inertia of the flywheel by applying a known gravitational torque (mgr) and measuring angular acceleration.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions focus on energy conservation, frictional torque correction, and calculation of moment of inertia.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torque as a Function of Angle (Work Done Graph)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting Torque (tau) versus Angular Displacement (theta).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area under the torque-angular displacement curve represents the total work done in rotating the body.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems involving variable restoring torques (like torsional pendulum).

solved_numericals.question: A force of 20 N is applied tangentially to the rim of a wheel of radius 0.5 m. Calculate the torque acting on the wheel.
solution_steps: Identify the given values: F = 20 N, r = 0.5 m, and since the force is applied tangentially, the angle theta between r and F is 90 degrees.
Use the torque formula: tau = r F sin(theta).
Substitute the values: tau = 0.5 * 20 * sin(90°) = 0.5 * 20 * 1 = 10 N·m.

solved_numericals.question: A uniform rod of mass M = 3 kg and length L = 2 m is pivoted smoothly at one end. It is released from rest in the horizontal position. Find the initial angular acceleration of the rod.
solution_steps: The weight of the rod acts downwards at its centre of mass, located at a distance r = L/2 from the pivot.
The magnitude of the gravitational torque about the pivot is tau = (Mg) * (L/2).
The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis passing through one end is I = (1/3) M L^2.
Using tau = I alpha, equate the expressions: (Mg L)/2 = ((1/3) M L^2) alpha.
Substitute g = 9.8 m/s^2 and L = 2 m: alpha = (3 * 9.8) / (2 * 2) = 29.4 / 4 = 7.35 rad/s^2.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 2 kg moves in the xy-plane with a position vector r = (3t i + 4t^2 j) m. Find the torque acting on the particle about the origin at t = 1 s.
solution_steps: Find the velocity vector by differentiating position with respect to time: v = dr/dt = (3 i + 8t j) m/s.
At t = 1 s, velocity v = (3 i + 8 j) m/s.
Calculate linear momentum p = m v = 2 * (3 i + 8 j) = (6 i + 16 j) kg·m/s.
Find position vector at t = 1 s: r = (3(1) i + 4(1)^2 j) = (3 i + 4 j) m.
Calculate torque as the rate of change of angular momentum or evaluate force if acceleration is known. Alternatively, find acceleration a = dv/dt = 8 j m/s^2, so force F = m a = 2 * (8 j) = 16 j N.
Calculate torque tau = r x F = (3 i + 4 j) x (16 j).
Compute cross product: (3 * 16)(i x j) + (4 * 16)(j x j) = 48 k N·m.

assumptions_and_limitations: Rigid body assumption: distances between constituent particles do not change under applied torque, which neglects internal deformations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Torque is a property of a single point in space.
common_misconceptions.correct: Torque is always defined with respect to a specific reference point or axis of rotation.
common_misconceptions.why: The position vector r depends entirely on the choice of the origin/pivot.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If the net force on a body is zero, the body cannot rotate.
common_misconceptions.correct: A body can experience zero net force yet have a non-zero net torque (forming a couple), resulting in angular acceleration.
common_misconceptions.why: Translational equilibrium (Sigma F = 0) does not guarantee rotational equilibrium (Sigma tau = 0).
